Market transformation does not occur overnight, and sometimes strategic intervention is necessary to accelerate technology adoption. 2.4.1.3 Challenge This challenge requires students to develop a holistic deployment solution that will increase market adoption of an emerging technology for building energy conservation and cost reduction. Teams will first select an emerging technology and a specific stakeholder group with limited adoption of the technology. Teams must then perform market research, identify adoption barriers through stakeholder engagement, and develop a holistic solution (technical, policy, and/or economic) to increase deployment. The solution must lead to higher market adoption rates and address barriers for the chosen stakeholder group. A holistic deployment solution—including technical and nontechnical aspects, such as policy and economic solutions—is required. 12 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. 3 Key Considerations Successfully attracting and training multidisciplinary talent to address current building challenges hinges on the process by which challenges are developed and implemented. Key considerations are presented from the perspective of challenge developers, implementers, and competition participants. By following the practices and processes discussed below, JUMP Into STEM has had a significant effect on the career choices and development of over 80% of participants (Rippy et al. 2022). 3.1 Challenge Development Topics for each challenge were identified through teaming sessions with academic and industry professionals. Working group members indicated key areas requiring new or increased research, and then program leadership selected final topics out of that list. This ensured that the challenges were relevant to immediate and emerging issues within building sciences. Finally, challenge descriptions were developed, which: • Emphasized direct connection to real stakeholder groups and consequences (e.g., high energy use or human health) • Warranted both a technical solution and one or more of the following components, as appropriate: economic, policy, commercialization, or other • Provided references and additional resources to support participants. 3.2 Challenge Implementation Team submissions were required to have a team background section and a challenge solution section. Participants discussed how their teaming structures incorporated multidisciplinary skill sets and majors, a key aim of the program. The latter section went into detail on the technical solution and market considerations. Participants also received evaluation criteria and a scoring rubric that mirrored the competition rules (see Section A.1). The criteria and rubric emphasized the weight of each element of the project while providing guidance for successful submission and scoring. In many cases, the challenges were implemented by professors in classroom settings, which broadened the reach and impact of the competition. No two implementation styles were the same, but notable practices that led to successful outcomes included: • Making participation in the competition voluntary so that students could develop skills in building sciences based on a personal disposition toward project- or competition-based learning • Providing resources and support to facilitate participation at all academic levels
